snippet.title: Why Do You Weigh Less at Earth's Equator?
snippet.description:
What If Earth Stopped Spinning?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6bbbvfCx6zY

Because the ground at the equator swings round so fast, you weigh about half of one percent less there than at the poles, and the whole planet bulges.

Sources: NGA Technical Report TR8350.2 (WGS 84), Table 3.4, equatorial gravity 9.7803 m/s² vs polar gravity 9.8322 m/s² (about 0.53% less) · NASA GSFC Earth Fact Sheet (Williams), equatorial radius 6,378.1 km vs polar radius 6,356.8 km (about 43 km wider across the equator). https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html

Pictures: NASA (ISS, DSCOVR/EPIC, GSFC Blue Marble), ESA/NASA (Alexander Gerst ISS time-lapse), ESO (La Silla Observatory time-lapse, CC BY 4.0), NOAA (GOES-16 satellite imagery), and Foucault pendulum footage, alongside AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA; ESA/NASA; ESO; NOAA.

snippet.title: How Close Will Gliese 710 Come to the Sun?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

Gaia measurements put Gliese 710's closest approach at about a fifth of a light-year — roughly 13,000 times the Earth–Sun distance. If the gap between the Sun and Earth were one centimetre, Neptune would sit 30 centimetres away on a ruler, and Gliese 710 would pass more than 100 metres away, the length of a football pitch.

Sources: Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 closest-approach distance of 10,635–16,649 AU (~0.21 light-years) (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a) · Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — Gliese 710 encounter and Oort Cloud scale (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835).

Pictures: NASA/JPL Voyager 2 full-disk photograph of Neptune (PIA01492), alongside original animated explainers, AI-generated scenes, and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: NASA/JPL.

snippet.title: What Will the Night Sky Look Like When Gliese 710 Arrives?
snippet.description:
What Happens When a Star Passes Through Our Solar System?
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F-jImX5h7ws

At closest approach in about 1.3 million years, the orange dwarf Gliese 710 will become the brightest star in the night sky — about three times brighter than Sirius, as bright as Jupiter at its best — and creep across the sky by the width of the full Moon every 35 years.

Sources: Berski & Dybczyński (2016), Astronomy & Astrophysics 595 L10 — peak brightness at magnitude −2.7 (about 3× brighter than Sirius) and perihelion proper motion of 52.28″/yr (~1 full-Moon width every 35.6 years) (https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201629835) · Bailer-Jones (2022), The Astrophysical Journal Letters 935 L9 — Gaia DR3 encounter distance and timing (https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ac816a).

Pictures: ESO La Silla night-sky and star-trails time-lapses by S. Brunier and R. Wesson (CC BY 4.0), NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA WISE infrared sky photograph, NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS Juno colour-enhanced photograph of Jupiter (PIA21974), and NASA/GSFC/ASU Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter full-Moon photograph, alongside original animated explainers and AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
Image credits: ESO/S. Brunier; R. Wesson/ESO; NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA; NASA/JPL-Caltech/SwRI/MSSS; NASA/GSFC/ASU.
